newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat seeks to pile pressure on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arafat seeks to pile pressure on Israel.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, worried Israeli settlement plans are destroying his people's dream of statehood, hopes to pile international pressure on the Jewish state at a Gaza meeting on Saturday.
Israel angered Arafat by announcing last month plans to build a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on a hill known in Arabic as Jabal Abu Ghneim and in Hebrew as Har Homa.
It enraged him further when it decided on a West Bank pullback that fell short of his expectations.

Arafat, under strong American pressure to prevent Palestinian frustrations from exploding into violence, has invited U.S., Arab, and European diplomats to Gaza on Saturday to discuss ways of salvaging peace talks.

However, the right-wing goverment of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday dismissed as "useless" a United Nations General Assembly call - approved by 130 votes to two - for Israel to cancel the building of the 6,500 homes.
Western diplomats also said the killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian soldier on Thursday eased the pressure temporarily on Netanyahu and may cast a shadow on Saturday's meeting.
Arafat has said the meeting will discuss "clear Israeli violations" of the Israel-PLO peace agreement "that undermine the peace process and threaten the whole Middle East".

Palestinians see Netanyahu's decision to build the houses for Jews in East Jerusalem as detrimental to their aspirations of establishing an independent state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip with East Jerusalem as capital.

Under the 1993 Israel-PLO peace accord, talks on a permanent settlement scheduled to resume later this month and end in 1999 would cover among other topics the future of Jerusalem and the fate of Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza.
The Israeli settlement announcement was received with warnings of a replay of last September's unprecedented Israeli-Palestinian gunbattles in which 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
Arafat has travelled the world campaigning for diplomatic pressure against the Israeli plans.

Palestinian Higher Education Minister Hanan Ashrawi said the Gaza conference, though it will be attended by low-level diplomats, is an "an attempt to create a system of accountability to try to rescue the peace process".
"We are trying now every possible means of averting a confrontation, by finding a political and diplomatic solution," said Ashrawi.
A United States decision to participate in the meeting, despite Israeli objections, has given added weight to the gathering, the first one of its kind in Gaza.
U.S. Republican party congressional leaders have said U.S. attendance is a mistake.

"The Palestinians are obviously very concerned at a number of recent developments and their impact on the peace process, whether it is the decision on Har Homa, Jabal Abu Ghneim or the Israeli decision on redeployment," U.S. Consul-General Edward Abington, who will attend the Gaza meeting, said on Thursday.

"We expect to meet with Chairman Arafat and his colleagues and to hear his views on the process and how to put it back on track and I'll report these views back to the Secretary of State and the President," he told reporters.
